title: Working at Redwood: roles, career ladders, benefits, hiring & onboarding, and internal tools
author: Ava Martinez
summary: A consolidated handbook page describing what it's like to work at Redwood, the role & career ladder framework, benefits and perks overview, hiring and onboarding process, and the canonical list of internal tools and access patterns.
content:
Overview

This document is the single-page reference for new and existing Redwoods about how we work, the career framework, core benefits, the hiring and onboarding workflow, and the internal tools you will use day-to-day. It is written for individual contributors, people managers, and hiring managers. Use the related links above for deeper policy pages and role-specific rubrics.

1) Working at Redwood — culture & expectations

Short intro: Redwood is an engineering-first company focused on production-grade LLM inference. Our operating rhythm and culture emphasize clarity of ownership, measurable outcomes, and continuous learning. Below are the behavioral expectations and day-to-day norms.

Core values (short):
- Be product-minded: ship value, not just features.
- Prioritize reliability and efficiency: latency/cost matter.
- Operate with radical clarity: document decisions and share metrics.
- Be a good teammate: help others succeed and ask for help early.

Day-to-day norms:
- Async-first communication: use Slack for urgent, Confluence for long-form, and PRs for design/code feedback.
- Weekly checkpoints: teams run a 30-minute sync and publish a short status note in the team channel.
- Ownership model: every service, dashboard, and runbook has a named owner in the team roster.

Working hours and flexibility:
- Core hours are 11:00–16:00 PT for most US-based teams; flexible scheduling across regions is supported.
- Remote-first policy with optional office desks for hybrid teams.

2) Roles and career ladders (summary and sample tables)

Purpose: We maintain leveled role families to provide transparency for expectations, promotion criteria, and compensation calibration. This section summarizes the IC (individual contributor) and Manager ladder and links to role-specific rubrics.

Level summary (IC and Manager families):

ASCII table:
| Level | IC Title (typical) | Manager Title (typical) | Core expectations | Promotion signals |
|-------|--------------------|-------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| L1    | Associate Engineer | N/A                     | Reliable task delivery, learns codebase | Completes onboarding milestones, regular PRs with reviews |
| L2    | Engineer           | Engineering Manager II  | Delivers features independently, owns small services | Repeatedly ships projects, mentorship activity |
| L3    | Senior Engineer    | Engineering Manager I   | Designs subsystems, influences cross-team work | Leads 1+ projects end-to-end, strong design reviews |
| L4    | Staff Engineer     | Engineering Manager II  | Architecture leadership, cross-org influence | Sets technical direction, successful program execution |
| L5    | Principal Engineer | Director / Senior EM     | Company-level strategy, deep domain expertise | Demonstrable impact on roadmap, hiring & retention influence |

Note: Titles and levels vary between teams (infrastructure, product, applied ML). Consult the team rubric for specific competencies and example behaviors.

Competency areas evaluated for promotion (short list):
- Technical execution and impact
- System design and breadth of ownership
- Collaboration and communication
- Mentorship and hiring
- Customer and product orientation (for product-adjacent teams)

Promotion process (high-level):
1. Candidate discusses growth with manager and sends self-nomination packet (summary, notable projects, feedback).
2. Manager assembles reviewers (peer, cross-functional, people-ops) and a promotion write-up.
3. Calibration meeting with Director-level + People Ops for final decision.
4. Communicate outcome and set development plan.

3) Benefits & perks (high-level summary)

Health & wellbeing:
- Medical, dental, vision plans with a company contribution (US/EU localized plans).
- 401(k) matching (US) / local retirement options per market.
- Mental health benefits: counseling stipend and access to an EAP provider.

Time off and leave:
- Generous PTO policy: baseline 20 days / year for full-time employees (pro-rated by region and local law).
- Parental leave: 16 weeks primary caregiver, 8 weeks secondary caregiver (region-dependent).
- Paid volunteer days and flexible holidays.

Financial & long-term incentives:
- Equity grants for full-time employees; refresh cycles during performance reviews and promotions.
- Competitive salary bands with transparent leveling.

Learning & career support:
- $2,000/year individual learning stipend (conference/trainings/books).
- Internal mentorship program and quarterly career workshops.

Work setup and allowances:
- Home office stipend on hire and hardware refresh policy (laptop + monitor).
- Commuter/office stipend for teams with office-based work (where applicable).

Perks and wellbeing programs (examples):
- Monthly wellness credit, team offsites budget, catered lunches for in-office days.

How to find details and eligibility:
- All plan documents, enrollment forms, and local policy variants live on the People Ops benefits portal (link in People Ops space).

4) Hiring & interview process (overview for candidates and hiring managers)

Goals: Fast, consistent, and unbiased hiring that results in high-quality new teammates. We use a structured interview process and documented rubrics to reduce bias and increase predictability.

Typical stages (standard IC role):
1. Requisition & intake: hiring manager and recruiter agree role profile, compensation band, and interview panel.
2. Phone screen (recruiter): confirms basic fit, salary expectations, authorization to work.
3. Technical screen (30–45m): short design/problem-solving exercise.
4. Onsite / loop (3–5 interviews, mix technical, system design, PMF, culture): structured questions per rubric.
5. Hiring debrief & calibration: panel submits feedback scores; hiring manager synthesizes.
6. Offer & negotiation: People Ops approves package and recruiter extends offer.
7. Background checks and references: initiated after offer acceptance (where required).

Interview best practices for interviewers:
- Use the shared rubric, score statements against evidence, and avoid hypothetical-only questions.
- Provide real-time feedback where helpful to candidates (timely follow-ups).
- Panel diversity: include cross-functional interviewers where possible.

Expected timelines: typical total cycle is 3–6 weeks from screen to offer for standard roles; critical or senior roles may take longer depending on panel availability.

Hiring manager checklist (brief):
- Confirm job description and band with recruitment partner.
- Curate interview panel and schedule loop.
- Prepare role-specific take-home or live exercises (if used).
- Ensure interviewers have read the rubric and candidate resume 48 hours prior.

5) Onboarding overview & 90-day plan

Objective: get new hires to meaningful contribution while setting long-term learning and career development expectations. Onboarding is a joint responsibility of People Ops, hiring manager, and onboarding buddy.

Pre-boarding (before start date):
- Offer acceptance tasks: complete paperwork, benefits enrollment window and submit ID for background checks.
- IT provisioning: laptop order, cloud account invites, Okta access, Slack invite.
- Pre-read packet: team charter, current roadmap, key repos, and first-week itinerary.

First day checklist:
- HR welcome meeting and benefits overview (People Ops).
- Manager 1:1 to review objectives and 30/60/90 plan.
- Setup accounts: GitHub, CI, Redwood Console, internal dev cluster, and Slack.
- Introductory team meeting and buddy assignment.

First week (sample):
- Week plan: context sessions (product, infra, applied-ml), security training, and first small onboarding task (bugfix or doc improvement).
- 30/60/90 goal setting meeting with manager.

First 90 days (milestones):
- 30 days: shipped first non-trivial contribution (PR merged) and completed security + compliance training.
- 60 days: owns a small feature or operational improvement, regular pairing with teammates.
- 90 days: demonstrated independent delivery, completed performance check-in and defined next development goals.

Onboarding owners:
- People Ops: benefits, payroll, paperwork, and new hire orientation.
- Hiring manager: technical ramp, goals, and feedback.
- Buddy: day-to-day navigation and practical tips.

6) Internal tools guide (canonical tools and access patterns)

Purpose: list the tools most new hires will need, who to contact for access, and common first tasks. If you need access beyond the defaults, submit an access request via the IT ticket queue.

Tools summary (short list):
- Slack — real-time communication. Channels: #company-announcements, #eng, #product, team channels. Use message threads and status updates.
- Confluence (this handbook) — policies and longer-form docs. Keep docs evergreen and link to related pages.
- GitHub — primary code host. Teams determine repo permissions; request membership via People Ops or team lead.
- CI/CD (Buildkite / CircleCI) — pipelines for tests and deploys, protected branches require 2 approvals.
- Redwood Console (internal) — deployment, model catalog, and telemetry dashboards. Access provided on request; SSO via Okta.
- Cloud Console (GCP/AWS) — read-only by default; write access requires justification and owner approval.
- PagerDuty — on-call routing for SRE and platform teams. On-call schedules in the SRE space.
- Okta / SSO — central auth provider. Use SSO to access GSuite, GitHub, Redwood Console, cloud consoles.
- Tools for collaboration: Figma (design), Notion (product briefs), Looker/Metabase (analytics).

Common access steps (commands / links) — quick reference:
1. Okta: Accept invite from people-ops, enroll MFA (recommended: hardware key or authenticator app).
2. Slack: join suggested channels; set profile and time zone.
3. GitHub: accept org invite, setup SSH key, confirm 2FA.
4. Redwood Console: request project access from your team lead; follow onboarding runbook for a demo token.

Security & compliance requirements for tools:
- MFA is required for all accounts with elevated privileges.
- Secrets: never commit keys to code. Use the Secrets Manager and follow the secret rotation schedule in the security space.
- Training: complete Secure SDLC and data classification training within first 14 days.

7) Practical examples & templates

Promotion self-nomination template (use in promotion packet):
- Summary of role and level sought.
- 3–5 Major outcomes in the last 12 months with measurable signals.
- Peer/manager feedback highlights (short quotes).
- Development plan if promoted.

Onboarding first PR template:
- Title: onboarding: fix <area> / add docs for <repo>
- Summary: short description, steps to run locally, test checklist.
- Owner & reviewers: list names and suggested reviewer.

Offer letter checklist (for hiring managers):
- Confirm band and equity with People Ops.
- Approvals: hiring manager, director, People Ops.
- Ensure background check vendor instructions are included in offer email (region-dependent).

8) Escalations and who to contact

People Ops general: people-ops@redwood.ai
IT / provisioning: it-support@redwood.ai
Security incidents: security@redwood.ai (also page on incident response in Security space)
On-call: see PagerDuty schedules in SRE space

9) Links and next steps

- People Ops benefits portal (enrollment & plan docs).
- Team-specific career rubrics (search the team space for ‘career rubric’).
- Onboarding runbook (detailed tasks and owners).
- Hiring / interview rubrics (interviewer training and scoring sheets).

Document maintenance: People Ops and People Ops partners should review this page quarterly or on major policy changes. If you find outdated information, open a Confluence edit request or message the page owner.
